transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

Well, I... I guess I'm just falling apart. I don't really know exactly where to start, to be honest, but it really all goes back to my daughter. She, uh, she just left for basic training. And I was so proud of her, I really was, but ever since she shipped out, it’s like... I don't know, it’s like I come home every day to a completely dead house. Just pure silence. And I just can't keep myself together at all. 

I mean, I’m a sheet metal worker, I've been doing this a long time and I'm supposed to be tough, but lately I’m sitting out in my truck in the shop parking lot before my shift just bawling my eyes out. Just crying before I even clock in. And it's bleeding into my work, which is honestly dangerous. I’m missing steps on welding jobs I’ve done for years—jobs I could usually do in my sleep—just completely blanking on the routine. Then the younger guys on the crew will ask me a simple question and I’m just snapping their heads off. It’s not fair to them and it's not like me. 

I don't even do the things I used to do to blow off steam. I used to love taking the boat out on the water, or going out to the garage and working on my metal sculptures, but I’ve completely stopped. I haven't touched any of it. I just sit there in the quiet because I just don’t see the point anymore without her around. I just can't seem to get a grip on myself.
Have you lost interest in activities you used to enjoy, like taking the boat out or working on your metal sculptures?

Yeah, I mean... I know I just said that, but it's really the truth. It's like... the boat, for instance. I've had that boat for, gosh, maybe six or seven years now. It's nothing fancy, just a little aluminum fishing boat, but my daughter and I used to take it out to the reservoir almost every other weekend when the weather was good. We'd pack a cooler, grab some sandwiches from the deli down the street, and just sit out there on the water for hours. It was our thing, you know? And I used to look forward to it all week. I'd be at the shop, sweating through my coveralls, just thinking about getting out on the water on Saturday. But now? The boat is just sitting under a tarp in the driveway. I look at it when I pull in from work, and I just feel... nothing. Or, well, I feel sad, I guess. But I don't feel any desire to actually uncover it and hitch it up to the truck. 

And the sculptures... that's a whole other thing. I started doing that as a way to use up scrap metal from the shop, just messing around with the welder in the garage. I made this big owl for my daughter's room a few years back, and she loved it so much that I just kept making things. Little animals, abstract pieces, whatever came to mind. It used to be my way to decompress after a long shift. I'd put on some music, put my hood down, and just get lost in the sparks and the metal. But the garage is just so quiet now. I went out there last week, thinking maybe I'd just tidy up the workbench, maybe organize my clamps, but I just stood there looking at my tools and I couldn't even bring myself to turn the radio on. It just feels so empty. Everything feels empty. So, yeah, I haven't done any of it. It's like the color just drained out of everything I used to like doing.
Would you say you’re feeling down or depressed most of the time now, even when you’re not thinking about your daughter?

Well, I mean... I don't know if I'd say I'm depressed *most* of the time when I'm not thinking about her, because honestly, I'm almost always thinking about her. It's like... even when I'm at work, you know? Like I was saying about the welding jobs. I'll be in the middle of a seam, sparks flying, hood down, and normally that's my zone. That's where I can just shut my brain off and let my hands do the work. I've been doing it since I was nineteen, straight out of high school. But now, even in the middle of that, my mind just drifts right back to her. I start wondering if she's eating enough, or if the drill sergeants are being too hard on her, or if she's lonely. 

So it's hard to separate the two, you know? Am I down because I'm just generally depressed, or am I down because she's all I can think about? I guess... I guess if I really try to think about moments where she's not actively on my mind... I don't know. Maybe? I just feel so heavy all the time. Like there's this physical weight on my chest, right here. And it doesn't really go away. Even when I'm just sitting at a red light on the way to the shop, listening to the blinker tick, I just feel this overwhelming sense of... I don't even know what to call it. It's just a dark cloud. 

But is it depression? I don't know. I've never really been a depressed person. I've always been the strong one, the one who fixes things. When my buddy at the shop broke his leg last year, I was the one organizing the meal train and covering his shifts. I don't do 'sad'. But now, it's just... it's all I feel. So I guess the answer is maybe? I'm sorry, I know that's not a straight yes or no, but it's just so tangled up in everything else right now.
Have you been feeling guilty or blamed yourself for things you couldn’t control, or felt like you’re not good enough since your daughter left?

Guilty? No, I wouldn't say guilty. It's not like I feel like it's my fault she left or anything like that. I mean, we talked about this for months before she actually signed the papers. She's always wanted to do something big, something important, and I've always told her she could do whatever she set her mind to. I was the one who drove her to the recruiter's office the first time, back in November. It was raining, I remember that, and we stopped for coffee on the way because she was so nervous her hands were shaking. I held her hand across the center console and told her how proud I was. 

So, no, I don't blame myself for her being gone. And I don't feel like I'm not good enough, either. I know I raised a strong, capable young woman. I was a single mom for most of her life, working my way up at the shop, taking all the overtime I could get just to make sure she had decent shoes for track season and could go on the school trips. I know I did a good job with her. 

It's just... it's not guilt, it's just this massive hole she left behind. It's like my whole identity for the last eighteen years has been 'mom'. Even at work, the guys call me 'Mama Bear' because I'm always bringing in baked goods or nagging them to wear their safety glasses. Being her mom is the best thing I've ever done. And now that she's just... not here... I don't feel guilty, I just feel lost. I don't know what I'm supposed to do with myself when I'm not taking care of her. Like, I bought a giant pack of toilet paper at Costco last weekend on autopilot, and when I got home and put it in the hall closet, I just broke down, because it's going to take me a year to go through that by myself. It's stupid things like that. So, no, not guilt. Just... emptiness.
Have you been having trouble sleeping lately, like trouble falling asleep, waking up during the night, or waking up earlier than you want and not being able to go back to sleep?

Well, honestly, sleep hasn't really been the issue. You'd think it would be, with my mind racing about her all the time, but... I don't know, my job is really physical. Being a sheet metal worker, I'm on my feet for ten, sometimes twelve hours a day. I'm lifting heavy sheets of aluminum and steel, running the press brake, wrestling with the shears... it takes a toll. By the time I clock out, my shoulders are just screaming and my lower back is completely shot. 

So when I get home... I mean, I go through the motions. I heat up whatever leftovers are in the fridge—lately it's just been canned soup or something easy because cooking a real meal for one just feels so pointless, like I was saying before—and then I take a long, hot shower just to get the grime and the metal dust out of my hair. And once my head hits the pillow... I'm just out. It's almost like my body just completely shuts down because it can't handle the physical exhaustion on top of the emotional exhaustion, you know? 

I sleep straight through, too. Actually, just the other night there was a massive thunderstorm, one of those really loud ones that rattles the windows and sets the dogs off down the street, and I didn't even hear a drop of it. My neighbor asked me about it the next morning when I was warming up my truck, and I had absolutely no idea what he was talking about. I was dead to the world. 

But then, waking up... that's the hard part. Not that I wake up too early or anything, I sleep right up until my alarm goes off at 5:00 AM. But when that alarm goes off, it's like... for a split second, I forget she's not here. I expect to hear her hair dryer running through the wall, or I think I need to go knock on her bedroom door to make sure she's up so she doesn't miss the bus. I even catch myself listening for her footsteps on the stairs. And then it just... it hits me all over again. The quiet. The house is just so incredibly quiet. So, yeah, I'm sleeping fine. Falling asleep right away, sleeping all the way through the night. It's just the waking up and having to face the empty house that's the problem, not the actual sleep itself.
Have you ever felt like life isn’t worth living or had thoughts about ending your life since your daughter left?

Oh, god, no. No, nothing like that. I mean, I know I've been sitting here telling you how heavy everything feels and how empty the house is, and I know I told you I cry over bulk toilet paper now, but... no. I would never do that. I could never do that to her. 

Think about it, she's out there in basic training, right? She's pushing herself to the absolute limit, probably getting yelled at, sleeping in a barracks with fifty other girls, just trying to prove she has what it takes. If I did something like that... if I just gave up... how could I ever justify that? Or worse, she'd get a visit from a chaplain or a commanding officer while she's in the middle of her training. I've heard how the military handles family emergencies, they pull you right out of your unit and it completely derails your progress. I spent eighteen years building her up, working all those double shifts so she could have a good life and spread her wings. I am absolutely not going to be the anchor that drags her down just because I can't handle my own house being quiet. 

Plus, I've got my guys at the shop. I know it sounds silly to bring up work again, but if I wasn't there, who's going to run the big Cincinnati press brake? We've got this one machine, it's older than I am, I swear, and it has this weird quirk where the backgauge sticks if you don't grease it exactly right on the left side. The new kids, the apprentices we just hired, they just jam it and mess up the calibration every single time. I'm the only one who really knows how to feather the foot pedal to get a perfect 90-degree bend on the thick gauge stainless. If I'm not there, the whole production line for the commercial HVAC ducting we're doing for that new hospital downtown would just grind to a halt. They need me. 

So, life is definitely worth living. It's just... it's just really, really uncomfortable right now. It's not that I want to die, or stop existing, it's just that I want things to feel normal again. I want to fast-forward to Thanksgiving when she gets her first leave and I can bake a turkey and have the house smell like sage and onions instead of just... dust and silence. So, no, definitely no thoughts of ending it. I just have to figure out how to get through the hours in the day until she comes home to visit. I just don't know how to do that yet. But I'm not going to do anything to hurt myself. I promise you that. I've always been a survivor.
Have you noticed any trouble concentrating or thinking clearly lately, like during conversations or while working on tasks?

Honestly, no, I haven't had any trouble with that. My head is pretty clear. I mean, in my line of work, you really can't afford to lose your focus or let your mind wander. I'm working with industrial shears that can slice right through a quarter-inch of solid steel like it's absolutely nothing. If I zone out for even a second, I could lose a finger, or someone else could get seriously hurt. 

Just yesterday, for example, we were working on this big custom duct run for that hospital job I was telling you about, and I had to read these incredibly detailed blueprints. The architect had spec'd out these weird transitional pieces, going from a square duct to a round one, with this strange offset because it has to dodge some plumbing pipes in the ceiling. It's a lot of complex geometry, especially for someone who just has a high school diploma, you know? You have to calculate the bend allowances, figure out the exact stretchout of the metal before you even make the first cut. I did all the math in my head, marked it all out with my scribe, and it fit perfectly on the very first try. My foreman, Dave, he even joked that my brain is a better calculator than the actual computer they have sitting in the front office. 

And as for conversations, I'm tracking everything just fine. I was talking to my sister on the phone for like two hours on Sunday afternoon. She was going on and on about this property line dispute she's having with her neighbor—which, honestly, is completely ridiculous because they're literally arguing over a lilac bush that's been dead for three years—but I remembered every single detail she had told me from three weeks ago about the surveyor they hired and what the city zoning guy said. I didn't lose the thread of the conversation once. 

So my brain works just fine. If anything, it's almost like... I want to be distracted, you know? When I'm at the shop, measuring and cutting and bending, my mind is one hundred percent focused on the metal. It has to be. And it's actually a huge relief to have to concentrate that hard, because it's the only time during the day that I'm not thinking about my daughter and how quiet my house is. The focus is kind of my only escape right now. If anything, my thoughts are way too clear when I get home. I just sit there on the couch and my mind just circles around every single thing I would be doing if she were still in her room. But no, no brain fog or trouble concentrating or anything like that. I'm sharp as a tack.
Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or on the contrary, have you been more restless or fidgety lately?

No, I haven't noticed anything like that. I mean, I'm definitely not moving in slow motion or dragging myself around, and my speech... well, you can hear me right now, I'm talking at my normal pace. I'm probably talking too much, honestly, but that's just how I've always been. 

At the shop, you really can't afford to be slow anyway. We have production quotas to meet, right? If my foreman, Dave, sees you lagging behind on the line when we're trying to push out a massive order of ductwork, he's going to be on your case in a heartbeat. You have to keep a steady rhythm—grab the sheet, line it up on the backgauge, hit the pedal, flip it, hit the pedal again. It's a whole dance. If you're moving like molasses, you throw off the guy next to you who's waiting to spot-weld the seams. So, physically, my body is keeping up the exact same pace it always has. 

And as for being restless or fidgety... no, not really. I'm not pacing the halls at night or tapping my foot constantly or anything like that. Honestly, when I get home, I just sit. I have this big brown recliner in the living room—I bought it on clearance a few years ago, it has a little scuff on the left armrest but it is just incredibly comfortable—and it's right across from the TV, though I rarely even turn the TV on lately. I just sink into it and I'll sit there for two, maybe three hours straight without really moving a muscle. 

It's not because I'm frozen or because my body is heavy, it's just because... well, what's the point of moving around? The house is spotless because nobody is there to make a mess, there's no teenager's laundry to gather up from the bathroom floor, no dinner to rush around cooking. So I just sit there and look at the wall. My hands are completely still. I don't feel jittery or like I have nervous energy to burn off. My sister, she's the fidgety one in the family, always clicking a pen or peeling the label off her water bottle when we're talking, but I've never been like that. So yeah, no slow motion, no pacing around. Just... regular movement, just with a lot less to actually do when I clock out.
Have you felt this way — down, empty, or losing interest in things — for most of the day, nearly every day, for at least two weeks in a row?

Yeah, definitely more than two weeks. It's been exactly... well, about a month now. She shipped out four weeks ago this past Tuesday. I remember because I had to take the whole morning off work to drop her off at the processing station downtown, the one right next to that old diner where we used to get pancakes on her birthdays. 

And literally, since the second I watched her get on that bus with all the other recruits, with her little duffel bag, I've just been struggling like this. It's been every single day since then. I drove home that afternoon, walked through the front door, and it was just... bam. The silence hit me like a physical weight. So, yes, most of the day, nearly every day. It's not like I have good days and bad days right now where it comes and goes. It's just one long, continuous stretch of feeling completely hollowed out. 

Like I was saying before, when I'm at the shop, I'm focused on the metal and the blueprints, so my brain is occupied, but that heavy feeling? It's still right there underneath it all, just waiting for me to clock out. And then I come home, and I sit in that brown recliner I told you about, and it's just... nothing. I don't want to watch TV, I don't want to work on my garden, I don't even want to cook a real meal. I've basically been eating cold sandwiches over the sink for a month because I just don't see the point of dirtying a pan for one person. 

So it's definitely been longer than two weeks. It's been a whole month of this. Thirty straight days of waking up, forgetting for half a second, and then remembering she's not in the next room, and just feeling that pit in my stomach all over again. I keep hoping I'll wake up on a Saturday and feel a little lighter, or maybe actually want to go out and do something, but... nope. It's just been this exact same heavy emptiness since the day she left.
Have you noticed a big drop in your energy level lately, like feeling tired all the time even after a full night’s sleep?

No, not really. I mean... my energy is completely fine. I'm definitely not walking around feeling physically exhausted or needing a nap or anything like that. 

I still wake up at 4:30 every single morning, usually about five minutes before my alarm even goes off. I've had this same old digital clock radio on my nightstand for probably fifteen years—the kind with those really obnoxious, bright red numbers and a buzzer that sounds like a fire alarm—but I almost always beat it. I just open my eyes, get up, make my one cup of black coffee, and head to the shop. 

And you have to understand, my job is incredibly physical. You're constantly hauling around these massive, awkward sheets of 18-gauge galvanized steel. They are heavy, and they can be really unwieldy, especially when you're trying to feed an eight-foot sheet into the shear by yourself, or when you're running pieces through the Pittsburgh lock machine. That takes a ton of upper body strength and leverage just to keep the metal feeding straight so the seams don't get all chewed up. Plus, you're standing on solid concrete for eight, sometimes ten hours a day if we're pulling overtime. 

If my energy was actually dropping, I would absolutely feel it. I'd feel it in my shoulders, or my lower back, or my legs. But physically? I can still outwork half the guys on the floor. I don't feel weak or fatigued at all. 

Like I was saying before about when I get home and sit in that brown recliner... I'm not sleeping when I'm in it. I'm not nodding off or struggling to keep my eyes open. I'm wide awake. My body has plenty of energy, it's just... I don't have anything to use it on anymore once I leave the shop. There's no softball practice to drive to, no running around the kitchen trying to get dinner on the table before she has to do her homework. It's not a physical exhaustion at all, it's just a complete lack of anything to do with the energy I have. So, yeah, no drop in energy. I'm just as strong and awake as I've always been.
Have you experienced a complete loss of pleasure or satisfaction from things you used to enjoy, like being on the water or creating metal sculptures?

Yeah... yeah, I have. Completely. I mean, I used to love taking my little aluminum boat out on the water on the weekends, just casting a line or even just sitting there listening to the water lap against the hull. It was my reset button. And my sculptures... I used to bring home scrap pieces from the shop, little off-cuts of copper and galvanized steel that were just going to the recycling bin, and I'd spend hours out in the garage welding them into these intricate abstract pieces. I’d put on my mask and just get lost in it, making something beautiful out of scrap. 

But now? I haven't touched my torch at home once. I haven't even looked at the boat. I’ve completely stopped going out on the water or working on my sculpture because... well, I just don’t see the point. 

Since my daughter left for basic training, it’s like all the color has just drained out of my life. I feel like I come home to a dead house every single afternoon. It’s so quiet it actually rings in my ears, and I just can’t keep myself together. It’s not just when I'm sitting in that recliner, either. It’s spilling over into everything. I find myself sitting in my truck in the shop parking lot before my shifts, just crying my eyes out with the engine running, desperately trying to wipe my face and pull it together before I walk through the bay doors. 

And even when I get inside, my head is just... it's a mess. I'm missing steps on welding jobs I’ve done for years. Basic, routine stuff that I could normally do blindfolded, I'm suddenly messing up because my brain is just stuck on this loop of her being gone. Then I get so frustrated with myself that I end up snapping at the younger guys on the floor. There's this one kid, barely twenty, he just asked me a simple question about the brake press the other day and I completely bit his head off. That is not who I am. I'm usually the one showing the new guys the ropes, taking them under my wing, you know? But right now, I just... I can't. I can't focus, I don't care about my art, I don't care about the lake. I'm just trying to get through the day, but I'm falling apart doing it.
Have you felt like nothing gives you pleasure anymore, not even things you used to really enjoy?

Well, yeah, I mean... that's exactly what I was just trying to explain about the boat and my metal sculptures. Like I just said, the answer is a hundred percent yes. Nothing gives me that spark anymore. 

I know I just went on a whole tangent about my welding and being out on the water, but it really is everything. It's not just the big hobbies that I've lost interest in. It's the little everyday things, too. Like, I used to really look forward to just sitting on the back porch with a cold beer after a ten-hour shift, you know? Just watching the sun go down over the neighbor's big oak tree, feeling a cool breeze after being stuck inside a hot, dusty, loud shop all day. That used to be the absolute best part of my evening. I'd sit out there and just decompress. 

But now? I don't even bother unlocking the back door. I haven't bought a six-pack since she left. I just come inside, drop my heavy work boots by the door, and go straight to that brown recliner I keep telling you about. I know I keep bringing up that chair, but it's basically become my whole entire world when I'm not at the plant. I just sit there and stare at the wall. I don't even have the desire to turn on the radio in my truck on the drive home anymore. I used to listen to the classic rock station, tap my fingers on the steering wheel, maybe sing along to some Bob Seger or Fleetwood Mac... now I just drive in total silence. 

So, yes, exactly like you're asking, and like I was just saying—there is absolutely zero pleasure in anything right now. You know when you take a bite of your favorite food and it just suddenly tastes like wet cardboard? That's what my whole life feels like. The things I used to love just feel completely pointless now. I really don't know how else to explain it, but the joy is just entirely gone from every single part of my day.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight since your daughter left, like eating a lot more or a lot less than usual?

No... no, not really. I mean, my weight hasn't budged a single pound, and I'm eating about the same amount as I always do. 

I still pack my little blue Igloo cooler every single morning at 4:45 with the exact same things I’ve been packing for years. I make a turkey and Swiss on whole wheat, grab a handful of those salty pretzel crisps, an apple, and a couple of bottles of water. You just have to eat when you do what I do. If you try to skip lunch while you're running the shear or wrestling with those huge sheets of steel, you're going to get lightheaded, and that's exactly how people lose a finger or drop a hundred pounds of metal on their steel-toe boots. So I force it down at noon when the lunch whistle blows, usually just sitting out by the loading dock. I don't really enjoy it, like I was saying earlier about the food just tasting like wet cardboard, but I make sure I eat it all so I don't pass out on the floor. 

And dinner... well, dinner is definitely different now because my daughter isn't here, but the amount I'm eating hasn't really changed. I used to make a whole production out of it, you know? We'd do spaghetti with homemade meatballs, or I'd fire up the grill out back and do chicken and corn on the cob. Now, I just can't bring myself to cook a real meal for one person. It just feels way too quiet and empty in that kitchen. Just standing at the stove makes my chest ache. So I'll just microwave a can of chunky soup or make some toast with peanut butter and take it straight to that brown recliner I keep talking about. 

But I'm still getting the calories in. My Carhartt work pants fit exactly the same as they did before she left for basic. The heavy leather belt I wear at the shop is still on the exact same notch it’s been on for three years. I know some people stop eating entirely when they get stressed out, or maybe they sit around and eat a whole bunch of junk food, but my body just keeps demanding the same fuel, even if my mind is completely falling apart. So, no, my appetite hasn't dropped off, and I haven't gained or lost anything. It's really just the joy of the food that's gone, not the actual eating part.
Have you felt like you’re in a deep emotional hole that you can’t climb out of, even when there’s no specific reason or trigger making you feel that way?

Well, hang on... no. Not for *no reason*. I mean, am I in a deep hole? Yeah, absolutely. I feel like I'm at the bottom of a well and someone threw away the rope. But it's not just out of nowhere, you know? It's not like I just woke up one morning and the sky was falling for no earthly reason. 

It is entirely, one hundred percent because she left. My daughter. That is the trigger. That is the *only* trigger. Before she packed up her green duffel bag and got on that bus for basic training, I was fine. I was completely, totally fine! We had our routine. I'd go to the shop, put in my hours cutting and bending steel, come home, and we'd figure out dinner. It’s just been the two of us for so long, you know? I had her when I was nineteen, so we practically grew up together. We were a team. She’s my whole world. 

So when you ask if I feel this way without a specific reason, I have to say no to that part. There is a massive reason. It’s like someone took the main support beam out of my house and now the whole roof is just caving in on my head. If she were still here, if her sneakers were still tripped over in the hallway, I wouldn’t be sitting in that brown recliner staring at the wall every night. I wouldn’t be crying in my truck in the shop parking lot. I wouldn’t be snapping at the new guys on the press brake. I'd be out in the garage with my welding torch, making my sculptures, or out on the lake in my boat. 

I know exactly why I'm a mess. It’s the quiet. It's the empty house. It's knowing she's hundreds of miles away getting yelled at by drill sergeants while I'm stuck here trying to figure out how to just exist in a house that feels completely dead. So, yeah, the hole is incredibly deep, and I really can't seem to climb my way out of it, but I know exactly how I fell in. If she walked through that front door right now, all of this—the crying, the brain fog at work, the complete lack of interest in everything—it would all just vanish.
Have you had a period lasting at least two weeks where you felt down or empty most of the time, even before your daughter left for basic training?

No, no, definitely not before she left. I mean... sure, I was a little stressed out leading up to it, just because there was so much to do, you know? We were running around getting everything on her packing list, dealing with the recruiter, making sure she had all her paperwork in order, and having going-away dinners... but I wasn't feeling down or empty. Not at all. I was actually managing okay before she shipped out. I was totally my normal self. I was still going into the shop, still enjoying my evenings on the porch, still feeling like... well, like a normal person. 

It really wasn't until after she was actually gone that everything just fell apart. And even then, it wasn't the exact second she got on the bus. The first week or so, I was just trying to keep busy, you know? I deep-cleaned the whole house, washed all her sheets, organized the garage... just trying to outrun the quiet, I guess. But then, it all just caught up to me. I'd say this all really started within a few weeks of her leaving for basic training. 

By week two or three, that's when that deep, empty hole I was telling you about just opened up and swallowed me whole. Once the reality set in that she was really gone and I was just here in this big, silent house all by myself... that's when the bottom dropped out. Before that, my head was completely above water. So, no, nothing like this ever happened before she left. It’s entirely tied to her shipping out and me just not knowing what to do with myself now.
Have you ever had a period in your life, before your daughter left for basic training, where you felt down, hopeless, or lost interest in things for at least two weeks in a row?

Like I was just saying a minute ago, no. Not ever. I know you're asking about my whole life now, but the answer is still exactly the same. I've never been through anything even remotely like this. 

I mean, sure, life hasn't always been a walk in the park. Like I told you, I had her when I was nineteen. Being a young single mom, trying to figure out how to pay rent, getting my start in the sheet metal trade when I was just twenty-two... it was exhausting. You get stressed, you get tired, you worry when the heating bill is too high or the transmission on the truck starts slipping. But feeling hopeless? Losing interest in things? No, never. Not for two weeks, not even for two days. 

I always had her to keep me going. If I had a terrible day at the shop—like if the foreman was riding my case about a quota, or I got a nasty burn from the welding torch—I'd just come home, and she’d be there, and we'd laugh and make dinner. I never just stopped caring about my life. I was always the one planning our weekend trips, getting the boat ready for the lake, making sure we went to the county fair every single August to get those awful fried Oreos she loves. 

Even when things were really hard, like when my dad passed away a few years back, I was sad, obviously. I grieved. But I didn't lose interest in my life. I didn't feel this... this heavy, dead weight. I still put on my work boots every morning, I still took care of my kid, I still went out to the garage and worked on my metal sculptures. I've always been the strong one, you know? The one who just puts her head down and pushes through whatever life throws at her. It's just that the good feeling only lasts for a split second before I'm right back to staring at the living room wall, listening to that refrigerator hum. No, no, not completely. Like I was just saying with the phone call, hearing her voice definitely brought me joy. I mean, it was the absolute highlight of my entire month. So the joy is still there, Doc. The pleasure is still there. It is not like my brain is broken or I am dead inside or something. So I can feel it. I definitely can still feel happy about things. It just does not stick around like it used to. It is like any good feeling just gets swallowed up by how empty the house is now.
